periods.name: Early hominins
periods.description: Late Pliocene. Australopithecus afarensis lives in East Africa. The oldest known stone tools (Lomekwi 3, ~3.3 million years ago) are older than the earliest known fossils of the genus Homo, so who made them is unknown.

periods.name: Early Pleistocene
periods.description: The Pleistocene begins ~2.58 million years ago. Early Homo appears in Africa and coexists with Paranthropus. By ~1.8 million years ago Homo is at Dmanisi in Georgia, the oldest hominin fossils known outside Africa, and later in China and Java.

periods.name: Middle Pleistocene
periods.description: Geologically ~774,000–129,000 years ago. Lineages diverge: the Neanderthal lineage appears in Europe, Homo erectus persists in Asia, and small-bodied hominins live on Flores. Evolution here is branching, not a ladder.

periods.name: Emergence in Africa
periods.description: The oldest fossils attributed to Homo sapiens, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, date to roughly 300,000 years ago. Early sapiens remains are spread across Africa.

periods.name: Early dispersals
periods.description: Fossils in the Levant show that Homo sapiens left Africa at least intermittently long before the main dispersal. How lasting these early groups were is debated.

periods.name: Main out-of-Africa dispersal
periods.description: Genetic evidence indicates that most present-day non-African populations descend from a dispersal roughly 50,000–70,000 years ago.

periods.name: Late Pleistocene
periods.description: Homo sapiens is present across Africa, Eurasia and Sahul. The Last Glacial Maximum peaks around 26,000–19,000 years ago.

periods.name: Holocene
periods.description: The current geological epoch, beginning at the end of the last glacial period. Farming emerges independently in several regions.

sites.name: Jebel Irhoud
sites.description: Fossils dated ~315,000 years ago (±34,000), currently the earliest attributed to Homo sapiens.

sites.name: Omo Kibish
sites.description: Omo I. Age estimates range from ~195,000 to a minimum of ~233,000 years depending on the study.

sites.name: Misliya Cave
sites.description: A modern-human maxilla dated ~177,000–194,000 years ago, among the earliest sapiens evidence outside Africa.

sites.name: Herto
sites.description: Crania from the Middle Awash dated ~154,000–160,000 years ago.

sites.name: Skhul
sites.description: Burials of early Homo sapiens at Mount Carmel, dated roughly 100,000–135,000 years ago.

sites.name: Qafzeh
sites.description: Early Homo sapiens burials near Nazareth, dated roughly 90,000–120,000 years ago.

sites.name: Jwalapuram
sites.description: Stone tools from before and after the ~74,000-year-old Toba eruption; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated.

sites.name: Tam Pa Ling
sites.description: Modern human skull dated to at least ~46,000 years ago.

sites.name: Grotte Mandrin
sites.description: Modern-human tooth and tools dated ~54,000 years ago; interpretation debated.

sites.name: Madjedbebe
sites.description: Occupation dated ~65,000 years ago by some, ~50,000 or less by others.

sites.name: Bacho Kiro
sites.description: Among the earliest Homo sapiens in Europe, ~46,000–44,000 years ago.

sites.name: Ortvale Klde
sites.description: Rockshelter recording Upper Palaeolithic occupation from ~42,000–38,000 years ago (approximate location).

sites.name: Lake Mungo
sites.description: Burials showing people in the Australian interior by ~42,000 years ago.

sites.name: Yana RHS
sites.description: Arctic Siberian site occupied ~32,000 years ago.

sites.name: Dzudzuana Cave
sites.description: Source of ~26,000-year-old Caucasus genomes (approximate location).

sites.name: White Sands
sites.description: Human footprints dated ~23,000–21,000 years ago; dating debated.

sites.name: Monte Verde
sites.description: Settlement occupied by ~14,500 years ago.

sites.name: Hadar
sites.description: Australopithecus afarensis fossils, including 'Lucy' (~3.2 million years ago).
sites.details: One of the richest Pliocene hominin localities. Lucy (A.L. 288-1), found in 1974, preserves about 40% of a skeleton and shows upright walking combined with a small brain. A.L. 333 preserves remains of at least nine individuals.

sites.name: Olduvai Gorge
sites.description: Fossils of Paranthropus boisei and Homo habilis (both ~1.8 million years ago), plus Oldowan and Acheulean tools.
sites.details: Olduvai's layered deposits record nearly two million years. The type specimens of Paranthropus boisei (OH 5, 1959) and Homo habilis (OH 7, 1964) come from the same period, a classic case of different hominins living side by side.

sites.name: Kokiselei 4
sites.description: The oldest known Acheulean handaxes, ~1.76 million years ago. No hominin fossils at the site. Location approximate.
sites.details: Large cutting tools shaped on both faces mark the beginning of the Acheulean. They are usually linked to Homo erectus because of their age and region, but no fossils were found with them.

sites.name: Dmanisi
sites.description: The oldest hominin fossils known outside Africa (~1.85–1.78 million years ago): early Homo, not Homo sapiens.
sites.details: Five skulls and other remains of early Homo, together with simple stone tools, lie beneath a medieval town in southern Georgia. They are usually assigned to Homo erectus in a broad sense. Their small brains (~550–775 cm³) and the large variation between individuals reshaped ideas about the first hominins to leave Africa. These people lived about 1.8 million years before Homo sapiens reached the Caucasus.

sites.name: Rising Star Cave
sites.description: More than 1,500 fossil elements of Homo naledi, ~335,000–236,000 years old.

sites.name: Kebara Cave
sites.description: Neanderthal occupation; the Kebara 2 skeleton (~60,000 years ago) preserves a hyoid bone.

sites.name: Denisova Cave
sites.description: Where Denisovans were identified from DNA; also occupied by Neanderthals, and later by Homo sapiens.
sites.details: A finger bone sequenced in 2010 revealed a previously unknown hominin group. The cave also yielded Denisova 11, the daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father, direct proof that the two groups met.

sites.name: Baishiya Karst Cave
sites.description: The Xiahe mandible (at least ~160,000 years old), identified as Denisovan by ancient proteins, at ~3,280 m altitude.

sites.name: Liang Bua
sites.description: Skeletal remains of Homo floresiensis (~100,000–60,000 years ago) and stone tools to ~50,000 years ago.

sites.name: Satsurblia Cave
sites.description: Upper Palaeolithic cave occupied before and after the Last Glacial Maximum; a ~13,300-year-old human genome. Location approximate.
sites.details: Satsurblia records hunter-gatherers in western Georgia around the coldest phase of the last Ice Age. The genome of a woman who lived ~13,300 years ago revealed a distinct 'Caucasus hunter-gatherer' ancestry that split from other West Eurasian groups tens of thousands of years earlier and later contributed to many populations of Western Eurasia.

sites.name: Kotias Klde
sites.description: Mesolithic rockshelter; a ~9,700-year-old human genome showing Caucasus hunter-gatherer ancestry. Location approximate.
sites.details: The Kotias Klde genome, together with Satsurblia, shows that the Caucasus hunter-gatherer population persisted in the region across several thousand years, from the late Ice Age into the Holocene.

sites.name: Gadachrili Gora
sites.description: Early Neolithic village with chemical evidence of grape wine in pottery, ~6000–5800 BCE. Location approximate.
sites.details: Residue analysis of pottery from Gadachrili Gora and nearby Shulaveris Gora (Shulaveri–Shomutepe culture) detected tartaric acid and related compounds, the chemical signature of grape wine, ~8,000 years ago. It is the earliest known chemical evidence of grape wine.
